stages.sub: Why a government spending boost can end up displacing private economic activity rather than adding to it.

steps.q: A government running a large deficit needs to borrow a lot of money. If it competes with firms for the same pool of savings, what is likely to happen to the price of borrowing?
steps.hint: Think of borrowing as competing bids for a limited pool of savings.

steps.q: At any point in time, an economy has a certain number of workers, machines and materials available to use. If government spending rises without any of these increasing, is there automatically more of them to go round?
steps.right: No, the total available stays the same
steps.wrong: Yes, more spending creates more workers and machines
steps.hint: Spending is just money changing hands; does it create new workers or machines on its own?

steps.q: You already know that when government borrowing raises interest rates, private investment falls. Now suppose the government hires builders and buys equipment for a new hospital, using workers and machinery from that same fixed pool. Can firms simultaneously hire those same workers and machines for their own projects?
steps.right: No, they must compete for the same limited workers and machines
steps.wrong: Yes, there is always spare capacity for both
steps.hint: Think about builders and materials being used on the hospital site instead of a private factory.

steps.q: A government raises spending to boost the economy, but the resulting higher interest rates and direct use of workers and materials reduce private investment and output by a similar amount. Does total output rise by as much as the government hoped?
steps.right: No, the private fall offsets much of the gain
steps.wrong: Yes, the full amount still gets added
steps.hint: If private spending falls roughly as much as government spending rises, what happens to the net effect?
